Abstract
Background: Triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index has come to be a 
new insulin resistance (IR) marker and has also been independently 
linked with peripheral artery disease (PAD). Rutherford Grade 5 
ischemia is characterized by localized tissue loss or active 
ulceration, with critically compromised perfusion, a high propensity 
for infection, and a narrow healing window—making it the most 
refractory and precarious tipping point in limb-salvage therapy, 
where progression to amputation is most likely. The present study 
attempted to evaluate the clinic utility of the TyG index in 
predicting the post-procedural wound healing of Rutherford grade 
5 ischemia. Methods: This analysis incorporated 98 cases of 
chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) classified as Rutherford 
grade 5, treated via endovascular approaches from January 2016 to 
December 2022. This study applied univariate logistic regression to 
discern independent predictors, alongside computing receiver 
operating characteristic (ROC) curves to evaluate prognostic 
accuracy 
for 
wound 
recovery 
after 
interventions 
in 
these 
individuals. For deeper analysis of contributing elements, the 
cohort was split retrospectively and randomly into training (n=68, 
70%) and validation (n=30, 30%) groups. Leveraging training set 
information, both univariate and multivariate logistic regressions 
enabled the formulation of a nomogram to forecast healing 
post-revascularization in Rutherford grade 5 ischemia. Assessment 
of the model's effectiveness involved ROC evaluations, calibration 
assessments, and decision curve analysis (DCA).
Results: The results showed that the TyG index was statistically 
significant in Rutherford grade 5 patients (p=0.011). Univariate 
analysis indicated that the TyG index was an independent risk 
factor (OR: 3.96, 95% CI: 1.33-11.73, p=0.013), and it’s area under

Introduction
Peripheral artery disease (PAD), primarily driven by atherosclerosis 
causing arterial narrowing or occlusion, ranks as the third most 
common vascular condition globally, following coronary and 
cerebrovascular diseases, affecting over 200 million individuals[1, 2]. 
Many patients are asymptomatic, with intermittent claudication as

ARTICLE IN PRESS


ARTICLE IN PRESS
4
the primary symptom when present. 
The Rutherford classification for chronic lower limb ischemia 
was proposed by Rutherford in 1986 and revised in 1997[3]. It is a 
grading method used to guide patient management and clinical 
research. This classification integrates patients' clinical symptoms 
with objective examination results and has now become a 
commonly used tool for assessing the severity of lower limb 
atherosclerotic occlusion. Patients with Rutherford grade 5 present 
with minor tissue loss or active ulceration[4, 5]. The 2019 Global 
Vascular Guidelines indicate that rest pain, ischemic ulcers or 
gangrene lasting for more than two weeks caused by chronic 
ischemia (Rutherford grades 4 to 6) are referred to as chronic 
limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), which may lead to amputation or 
even death in severe cases[6].
 Accurate assessment of CLTI severity and identification of risk 
factors for impaired wound healing are critical for improving 
patient outcomes. Insulin resistance (IR) is a key driver in the 
progression of atherosclerosis, contributing to the development of 
PAD and other cardiovascular conditions[7]. While hyperinsulinemia 
has been linked to vascular changes, including endothelial 
dysfunction 
and 
increased 
arterial 
stiffness[8, 
9], 
the 
pathophysiology of IR in PAD is complex. The traditional "gold 
standard" — the hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp (HEC) — is 
precise but technically challenging and costly procedure, limiting 
its 
large-scale 
clinical 
application[10]. 
In 
contrast, 
the 
triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index, which combines fasting glucose 
and triglyceride levels, provides a more practical and cost-effective 
alternative for evaluating IR, especially in resource-limited settings. 
This index has shown promise for rapid risk stratification in clinical 
scenarios 
like 
Rutherford 
grade 
5 
ischemia, 
where 
swift 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ARTICLE IN PRESS


ARTICLE IN PRESS
5
intervention is critical[11, 12]. Previous studies have demonstrated 
that an elevated TyG index is associated with poorer recovery and 
prolonged healing in conditions such as spontaneous intracerebral 
hemorrhage[13]. However, its potential role in wound healing 
following endovascular treatment for CLTI remains unexplored. To 
fill this research gap, this study included 98 patients with 
Rutherford grade 5 CLTI. A uniform collection of metabolic 
indicators, lipid, inflammatory, and biochemical markers, including 
the TyG index, was performed to compare patients with "early 
healing" and "delayed healing" outcomes. Based on these data, a 
nomogram model was developed incorporating the TyG index, 
triglyceride (TG) levels, and smoking status. The clinical value of 
the model was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic 
(ROC) curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis (DCA). 
This nomogram aims to provide clinicians with a tool for 
personalized risk assessment, enabling early identification of 
high-risk patients, which could facilitate prompt intervention and 
optimize management strategies. By improving wound care and 
reducing the need for secondary interventions, this model has the 
potential to lower amputation rates, shorten hospital stays, and 
reduce healthcare costs.
Methods
Study Design and Patient Selection
This was a retrospective, observational study conducted at the First 
Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University from January 2016 
to December 2022. Since model construction is required in the 
later stage, we used the event-to-variable ratio (EPV) method to 
determine the sample size. The calculation formula is [minimum 
sample size=number of final model variables × 10][14]. It is

that 
the 
independent 
variables 
included

multivariate model will be ≤4 (TyG, TG, smoking, and one 
covariate), requiring at least 40 cases of 'delayed healing' events. 
Based on preliminary data, the postoperative delayed healing rate 
of Rutherford grade 5 patients is approximately 70%, so at least 
40/0.7≈57 cases are needed. Considering a 20% loss to follow-up 
and external validation, a total of 98 cases will be included (68 for 
training and 30 for validation), which meets the model stability 
requirements. A total of 98 patients diagnosed with chronic 
limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) and classified as Rutherford 
grade 
5, 
who 
underwent 
endovascular 
treatment 
during 
hospitalization, were included. These patients were divided into 
two groups based on wound healing time within one year after 
endovascular treatment for Rutherford grade 5: 28 patients with 
early wound healing and 70 patients with delayed wound healing.

Data Collection and main definitions
Based on the electronic medical records and imaging data, we 
collected the following information for each patient: gender, age, 
current medical history, past medical history, personal history,

laboratory test results, and WIFi (Wound Ischemia and Foot 
Infection) classification. Laboratory test results obtained after 
hospital admission, such as complete blood count and biochemical 
tests, were also recorded. Fasting venous blood samples were 
collected from the antecubital vein after a 12-hour fast. The 
following parameters were measured: White blood cell count 
(WBC), Red blood cell count (RBC), Platelet count (PLT), 
Neutrophil count (NEUT), Lymphocyte count (LYC), Mean platelet 
volume (MPV), Fasting plasma glucose (FPG), Total cholesterol 
(TC), Triglycerides (TG), High-density lipoprotein cholesterol 
(HDL-C), Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), Creatinine 
(Cr), Homocysteine (HCY), and Erythrocyte sedimentation rate 
(ESR). To avoid potential bias, the wound healing status was 
assessed by wound care specialists who were independent of the 
research team. These specialists were blinded to the specific TyG 
values of the patients during the assessment. This measure was 
designed to minimize assessment bias and ensure the objectivity of 
the results.
The calculation formulas are as follows:
TyG=Ln[（TG)（mg/dL）×FPG（mg/dL）/2]
NLR=NEUT/LYC

Main definitions are as follows:
Wound healing: Complete epithelialization of all wounds 
without major amputation[12].
Early 
healing: 
Wound 
healing 
time 
≤3 
months 
after 
endovascular treatment in Rutherford grade 5 patients. The

3-month cut-off was pre-specified according to the median healing 
time (76 days, IQR 58-105) observed in our cohort, and clinical 
practice in our centre where revascularisation efficacy is routinely 
reassessed at 12-week follow-up.
Delayed healing: Wound healing time > 3 months after 
endovascular treatment in Rutherford grade 5 patients.
Complete healing: The wound is fully epithelialized, with no 
necrosis, good structure and function, and no infection.
Effective healing: The wound area is reduced by ≥25% but 
<75%, with visible fresh granulation tissue and some relief of 
symptoms.
Ineffective healing: The wound area is reduced by <25%, with 
no significant improvement observed.
Primary outcome: Poor wound healing (the predicted outcome 
of the nomogram) was defined as failure to achieve complete 
wound epithelialization or major amputation (above the ankle) 
within 6 months after the index endovascular procedure.
Major amputation: Amputation performed above the level of the 
ankle joint.
Diabetes Mellitus: Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (≥ 7.0 
mmol/L), non-fasting glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (≥ 11.1 mmol/L), or 
self-reported

Surgical Methods and Follow-up
Perioperative treatment and endovascular treatment: Detailed 
records were maintained regarding the specifics of the patients' 
wounds, including the location, size, presence of infection, and 
presence of gangrene. In cases of concomitant infection, blood 
cultures were performed, and antibiotic therapy was administered 
based on the results. Routine dressing changes were conducted for 
open wounds, and in cases of severe infection, patients were 
referred to the wound repair center for local debridement and 
specialized wound care. According to the Global Vascular 
Guidelines for CLTI, patients were administered antiplatelet 
therapy and lipid-regulation treatment to stabilize plaques. 
Additionally, patients with comorbid hypertension or diabetes 
received concurrent treatment to control their blood pressure and 
blood glucose levels. All endovascular treatments included in this 
study were performed by chief or associate chief physicians with 
over 15 years of experience, uniformly based on the Angiosome 
concept[15]. Angiosome-based revascularization has emerged as the 
predominant strategy for patients with severe lower extremity 
ischemia. Angiosome refers to a three-dimensional tissue block 
perfused by a single source artery and its accompanying veins[16]. 
The goal of endovascular treatment was to establish at least one 
direct blood-supplying artery from the origin of the superficial 
femoral artery to the affected angiosome in the foot.

Postoperative 
follow-up: 
After 
discharge, 
patients 
were 
instructed to strictly abstain from smoking and limit alcohol 
consumption, actively manage their blood pressure and blood 
glucose levels, and continue wound dressing changes. For patients 
with extensive tissue loss or severe infections, further standardized 
wound repair treatment was conducted in a specialized wound 
repair department. We recorded contact information for patients or 
their family members and conducted follow-up assessments 
through outpatient visits or telephone calls at 1, 3, 6, and 12 
months post-operation. Follow-up evaluations included symptom 
improvement, wound healing progress, healing time, occurrence of 
major amputations, incidence of major adverse cardiovascular or 
cerebrovascular events, and patient survival status.
Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the Ethics 
Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical 
University 
[PJ-KS-KY-2024-423]. 
All 
study 
procedures 
were 
conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of 
Helsinki. As this was an observational, retrospective study without 
interventions or invasive procedures and did not involve the use of 
human physiological specimens, written informed consent was 
obtained from all study participants or their legal representatives, 
ensuring compliance with ethical standards.
Statistical analysis
We employed the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test in this study to assess 
the normality of the data. For continuous variables, the data were 
presented as mean±standard deviation or median (interquartile 
range), and comparisons of baseline variables were made using the 
unpaired t-test for normally distributed data or the Mann-Whitney 
U test for non-normally distributed data. Categorical variables were 
expressed as frequencies (percentages) and compared using the

ARTICLE IN PRESS


ARTICLE IN PRESS
11
chi-square test. Univariate logistic regression was used to screen 
for significant variables, and evaluate the risk factors for wound 
healing time following endovascular treatment in patients with 
Rutherford grade 5. Additionally, receiver operating characteristic 
(ROC) curves were constructed. It should be noted that among our 
98 cases, HbA1c information was missing in 70 cases (71.4%), 
D-Dimer information was missing in 3 cases (3.0%), and CRP 
information was missing in 10 cases (10.2%). In the statistical 
analysis, we ignored the missing values for these variables, i.e., a 
deletion method was adopted, while the analysis of the remaining 
variables was based on complete data.
A total of 98 patients were enrolled and randomly divided into a 
training cohort (n=68, 70%) and a validation cohort (n=30, 30%) 
for further analysis. In the training cohort, we performed univariate 
logistic regression analysis for variable selection and data 
dimension reduction. Based on the results of the univariate analysis, 
we conducted multivariate logistic regression analysis to develop a 
predictive model and construct a nomogram. We assessed the 
model's discriminatory ability using the area under the ROC curve 
(AUC). We evaluated the agreement between predicted and actual 
outcomes using the Hosmer-Lemeshow (X2) test and calibration 
curve plotting. We used decision curve analysis (DCA)[17] to assess 
the clinical utility of the diagnostic model. \* MERGEFORMAT

Baseline characteristics
28 of 98 patients (28.6%) achieved early wound healing, while 70 of

1. 
Logistic Regression Analysis of Risk Factors for Wound 
Healing Time in Rutherford Grade 5 Patients
Univariate logistic regression analysis was performed with wound 
healing time after endovascular treatment in Rutherford grade 5 
patients as the dependent variable and each independent variable 
as the predictor (Table 2). Variables with a p-value less than 0.05 in 
the univariate analysis were further included in the multivariate 
logistic regression model. The results indicated that the TyG index 
(OR: 3.96, 95% CI: 1.33-11.73, p=0.013) was an independent risk

factor for delayed wound healing in these patients.
The ROC Curve Analysis of TyG Index for Predicting Delayed 
Wound Healing
We assessed the clinical value of the TyG index in predicting wound 
healing after endovascular treatment in Rutherford grade 5 
patients using ROC curve analysis (Figure 1).The area under the 
ROC curve (AUC) was 0.68 (95% CI: 0.56-0.81), with a best cutoff 
value of 8.83, sensitivity of 67.1%, and specificity of 71.4%.
Multivariable Selection for Prediction Model
A total of 98 patients were enrolled and randomly divided into a 
training cohort (n=68, 70%) and a validation cohort (n=30, 30%) 
for further analysis. Univariate logistic regression analysis was 
conducted in the training cohort, identifying seven variables: TyG, 
TG/HDL-C, TC, TG, FPG, LDL-C, and smoking (Table 3). 
Multivariate logistic regression analysis, performed using the 
variables selected through univariate analysis, demonstrated that 
three factors were independently associated with wound healing 
following endovascular treatment in Rutherford grade 5 patients: 
TyG (OR=132.17, 95% CI: 1.15-15131.02, p=0.043), TG (OR=0.01, 
95% CI: 0.00-0.84, p=0.041), and smoking (OR=0.20, 95% CI: 
0.04-0.99, p=0.049).
Nomogram Development
We conducted a multivariate logistic regression analysis in the 
training cohort to identify independent predictive factors, which we 
then used to construct a nomogram (Figure 2). In clinical practice, 
the total score is calculated by adding the scores of TyG, TG, and 
smoking status, which is then projected onto the "risk" axis to 
determine the probability of delayed healing within 3 months. A 
score of 41 corresponds to a 50% predicted probability and is set as 
the decision threshold. Patients with a score ≥41 are considered

"high risk" and may require early interventions, while those with a 
score <41 are "low risk" and can follow standard care with regular 
follow-up.
Model Evaluation
We then assessed the model's performance using the validation 
cohort. The AUC indicated the nomogram's discriminative ability, 
with the value of 0.83 in the training cohort and 0.68 in the 
validation cohort (The internal bootstrap validation can be found in 
Figure S1, Figure S2 and Figure S3 from the file named 
"Supplementary Materials 1"). No significant difference was 
observed between the two cohorts, suggesting that the nomogram 
demonstrated strong sensitivity and specificity in a clinical setting 
(Figure 3). The calibration curve confirmed good concordance 
between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes (Hosmer–
Lemeshow test, p>0.05) (Figure 4). We performed DCA in the 
training (probability cutoff: 0.81) and validation (probability cutoff: 
0.86) cohort to evaluate the net clinical benefit of the prediction 
model (Figure 5). The application of this nomogram could improve 
risk 
assessment, 
address 
overlooked 
factors, 
and 
improve 
treatment 
strategies, 
potentially 
leading 
to 
better 
clinical 
interventions.
Discussion
This study analyzed the risk factors influencing wound healing time 
after endovascular treatment in patients with Rutherford grade 5. 
Following consistent endovascular treatment, the results indicated 
that the TyG index was an independent risk factor for wound 
healing in these patients. 
Although traditional cardiovascular risk factors—including 
smoking, 
diabetes, 
hypertension, 
and 
dyslipidemia—are 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ARTICLE IN PRESS


ARTICLE IN PRESS
15
well-established contributors to the development of peripheral 
artery disease (PAD), our analysis based on ischemic severity did 
not identify a direct association between these factors and wound 
healing following endovascular therapy in patients classified as 
Rutherford grade 5. The ankle-brachial index (ABI), which is the 
ratio of the ankle systolic pressure to the brachial artery systolic 
pressure, is one of the important non-invasive indicators for 
assessing atherosclerosis[18]. It was first proposed by Winsor in 
1950 and has been used for the diagnosis of PAD. Recent studies 
have found a negative correlation between the TyG index and ABI, 
suggesting that the TyG index may be a novel indicator for 
assessing the severity of atherosclerosis[19]. Studies have shown 
that the TyG index is not only closely associated with PAD but also 
significantly related to the incidence and severity of various 
cardiovascular diseases such as stroke, coronary heart disease, and 
hypertension[20-22]. Insulin resistance has a central role in 
atherosclerotic disease and has a close relationship with impaired 
or delayed wound healing. Previous studies have indicated that 
insulin resistance can lead to metabolic disturbances[23], including 
disruptions in glucose and lipid metabolism, which cause 
irreversible endothelial damage[24] and thereby affect tissue repair 
and regeneration capabilities. Post-procedural wound healing 
depends on adequate blood circulation and sufficient tissue 
nutritional 
support[25], 
while 
insulin 
resistance 
can 
induce 
microvascular dysfunction and local tissue hypoxia, thus delaying 
the healing process[26, 27]. In our study, the TyG index significantly 
may delay wound healing through the "insulin resistance-metabolic 
disorder-microvascular inflammation" cascade (Figure 6). First, 
high TyG reflects persistent insulin resistance, leading to 
hyperglycemia and hypertriglyceridemia: hyperglycemia inhibits 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ARTICLE IN PRESS


ARTICLE IN PRESS
16
neutrophil 
chemotaxis 
and 
blocks 
keratinocyte 
proliferation 
through advanced glycation end-products (AGEs)[28], while elevated 
triglycerides damage microvascular endothelium through excess 
reactive oxygen species[29]. Second, insulin resistance reduces 
endothelial nitric oxide production, leading to inadequate capillary 
perfusion, local hypoxia, and inhibition of fibroblast proliferation 
and collagen deposition. Furthermore, inflammation plays a key 
role in the wound healing process, and the TyG index may be a 
sensitive indicator of vascular aging and the extent of vascular 
involvement. Studies have shown that the TyG index serves as an 
independent predictor of PAD severity and complexity[30]. A higher 
TyG index may activate inflammatory pathways[31], leading to 
intensified local and systemic inflammatory responses that 
negatively 
affects 
wound 
healing. 
Therefore, 
elevated 
TyG 
increases the risk of delayed healing and amputation, providing a 
simple and cost-effective early intervention target for clinical 
practice.
In patients with Rutherford grade 5 PAD, delayed wound 
healing was associated with significantly higher TG/HDL-C ratios, 
as well as elevated TG and FPG levels, compared to those with 
early healing. One possible explanation is that in obese individuals, 
the avascular adipose tissue around wounds may diminish 
resistance to infection under hypoxic conditions and impair cellular 
repair mechanisms, thereby further delaying healing.[32]. Elevated 
blood glucose levels can induce peripheral neuropathy, which not 
only diminishes foot sensation but also impairs granulation tissue 
formation. Additionally, diabetic patients are at higher risk of 
secondary wound infections, both of which adversely affect wound 
healing[33]. Furthermore, the healing of lower limb ulcers is 
influenced by multiple factors, including patient comorbidities (e.g., 
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ARTICLE IN PRESS


ARTICLE IN PRESS
17
diabetes, 
hemodialysis, 
coronary 
artery 
disease), 
wound 
characteristics (location, depth, and size), postoperative activity 
levels, medication adherence, lifestyle, and overall quality of life[34].
As an inflammatory marker, NLR has been widely applied in 
various systemic diseases and has shown unique sensitivity in 
atherosclerotic diseases[35]. Li[36]compared the angiographic results 
of patients with PAD and found a significant correlation between 
NLR and the degree of vascular stenosis. Another meta-analysis 
including 5,243 patients with PAD showed that elevated NLR is 
associated 
with 
mortality, 
amputation, 
and 
major 
adverse 
cardiovascular events, demonstrating the important prognostic 
value of NLR in PAD patients[37]. NHR, PHR, and SII are recently 
discovered indicators that can reflect both inflammation and lipid 
metabolism and have gradually attracted academic attention. 
Song[38] found that NHR, PHR, and SII are higher in diabetic 
patients with PAD, with statistical significance, and these 
indicators have predictive value for the occurrence of diabetes 
combined with PAD, indicating a close relationship with the 
development of PAD. However, in this study, NLR, NHR, PHR, and 
SII did not show predictive ability in assessing wound healing after 
endovascular treatment in Rutherford grade 5 patients.
Despite the extensive research on the diagnosis, progression, 
and severity of CLTI, there is still a lack of studies on wound 
healing in these patients after endovascular treatment. The current 
WIfI 
classification 
(Wound, 
Ischaemia, 
and 
foot 
Infection) 
integrates wound extent, severity of ischemia, and foot infection to 
stage disease acuity, while the ABI provides a general estimate of 
limb perfusion. However, neither system specifically quantifies the 
metabolic-inflammatory environment that may delay wound healing 
after revascularization. The inclusion of the TyG index—along with

its 
easily 
measurable

(fasting 
glucose 
and 
triglycerides)—appears to capture this risk, thereby offering 
incremental value for early identification of patients who may 
require intensive metabolic management or preventive treatment. 
This study analyzed the relationship between the TyG index and the 
post-procedural wound healing of Rutherford grade 5 patients and 
identified a convenient and cost-effective method for assessing the 
clinical outcomes of these patients. According to the DCA curve in 
this study, both the training set (probability cutoff: 0.81) and the 
validation set (probability cutoff: 0.86) show that, within the low to 
moderate cost-effectiveness ratio range, the net benefit curve of 
the nomogram model is generally above the "no intervention" curve. 
This indicates that, at these cost-effectiveness ratios, using this 
model to guide treatment may provide additional benefits to 
patients. For instance, applying the TyG index-based nomogram 
model in the low cost-effectiveness ratio range allows for more 
accurate identification of Rutherford grade 5 patients at higher risk 
of poor healing, enabling healthcare teams to intervene earlier. 
Conversely, for low-risk patients, it helps avoid unnecessary 
overtreatment, reducing both healthcare resource waste and the 
economic and psychological burden on patients. It should be note 
that, after internal bootstrap validation, the AUC remains relatively 
stable after calibration, but the calibration slope is quite high at 
4.870917. In the future, cross-validation, model adjustments, or 
other methods may be needed to further improve the model's 
stability and accuracy.
However, our findings still have many limitations. Firstly, this 
study is a single-center retrospective study with a relatively limited 
sample size, and the analysis was conducted solely within the case 
cohort without external cohort validation. The use of a single

cohort may also introduce specific selection bias due to the 
exclusion of outpatient and primary care settings, limiting the 
generalizability of the model. Secondly, the follow-up period of this 
study is one year, lacking long-term follow-up data, and thus unable 
to analyze the predictive value of the TyG index for long-term 
prognosis. Thirdly, this study only collected the TyG index before 
endovascular treatment and did not monitor the dynamic changes 
of the TyG index after surgery, which may impose certain 
limitations on the study results. What’s more, this study did not 
analyze the TyG index in relation to patency rates, in-stent 
restenosis 
and target 
lesion revascularization, 
indicating 
a 
relatively limited scope of research. It is also important to note that 
in the multivariate model, TyG has a high odds ratio (132.17) with a 
wide confidence interval (1.15-15131.00), which reflects the small 
sample size (only 68 cases in the training set). This result may be 
amplified by extreme samples, and further validation in a 
multi-center large cohort is needed, along with the use of penalized 
regression or Bayesian shrinkage methods to reduce the risk of 
overfitting. We used the logistf package[39] to perform Firth 
penalized regression to attempt to eliminate extreme estimates 
caused by small sample sizes. After shrinkage, the OR for TyG was 
2.83, much smaller than the 132 reported in the original 
manuscript. yet it still exhibited an extremely wide 95% confidence 
interval 
(1.42-311.64) 
(Table

from

named 
"Supplementary Materials 2"). Although our results remain 
statistically significant to some extent, the considerable width of 
the confidence interval limits the interpretability of the findings, 
which should therefore be interpreted with caution. Furthermore, 
multivariate 
analysis 
unexpectedly 
revealed 
a 
"protective 
association" between smoking and postoperative wound healing,

which contradicts intuition, as smoking is typically associated with 
impaired vascular health and theoretically should increase the risk 
of delayed healing. The small sample size may have led to 
overfitting of the model, which could affect the interpretation of the 
results. Additionally, there may be confounding due to the 
distribution of smoking status and gender, as more male 
participants were smokers compared to females, which could 
manifest as a protective effect of smoking in the model. Therefore, 
in this study, the smoking factor remains exploratory and should 
not be interpreted causally. Future studies should expand the 
sample size and control for confounding factors to validate the true 
impact of smoking on healing. Moreover, the nomogram model 
performed well in the training cohort, but the AUC value in the 
validation cohort was relatively low. The possible reason is the 
small sample size, which may have led to an overestimation of OR 
and population heterogeneity (e.g., a higher proportion of diabetic 
women). Additionally, the proportion of male smokers is generally 
higher than that of female smokers, and the small sample size may 
have resulted in instability in clinical characteristics. Finally, with a 
74% missing rate in HbA1c data, deletion methods were used and 
may cause bias, imputation or prospective validation should be 
employed in the subsequent studies. Future studies should include 
multi-ethnic samples through prospective multi-center large cohort 
research, apply LASSO/ridge regression combined with Bootstrap 
for coefficient shrinkage, and establish a quarterly dynamic 
calibration mechanism to continuously correct population drift and 
enhance the applicability of this nomogram model. Long-term 
follow-up of patients should be also conducted, and prospective, 
multicenter clinical trials should be carried out. In addition, the 
combined 
application 
of 
the 
TyG 
index 
with 
other

metabolism-related 
indicators 
should 
be

to 
comprehensively assess its value in symptom improvement, wound 
healing, vascular patency, revascularization, amputation, and 
mortality in CLTI patients.
Conclusion
The TyG index may be an independent risk factor for delayed 
wound healing in Rutherford grade 5 patients post-surgery and 
have good predictive value for postoperative wound healing. The 
nomogram model, developed using the TyG index, TG levels, and 
smoking status, may offer a useful tool for estimating healing risk 
in clinical settings, potentially assisting in clinical decision-making. 
Future multi-center prospective studies with larger sample sizes, 
dynamic postoperative TyG monitoring, and annual recalibration of 
weights 
are 
expected 
to 
guide 
wound 
management 
and 
personalized interventions for Rutherford grade 5 patients, thereby 
reducing 
amputation 
rates, 
shortening 
hospital 
stays, 
and 
optimizing healthcare resource utilization.

Abstract: Background: Triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index has come to be a new insulin resistance (IR) marker and has also been independently linked with peripheral artery disease (PAD). Rutherford Grade 5 ischemia is characterized by localized tissue loss or active ulceration, with critically compromised perfusion, a high propensity for infection, and a narrow healing window—making it the most refractory and precarious tipping point in limb-salvage therapy, where progression to amputation is most likely. The present study attempted to evaluate the clinic utility of the TyG index in predicting the post-procedural wound healing of Rutherford grade 5 ischemia. Methods: This analysis incorporated 98 cases of chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) classified as Rutherford grade 5, treated via endovascular approaches from January 2016 to December 2022. This study applied univariate logistic regression to discern independent predictors, alongside computing receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves to evaluate prognostic accuracy for wound recovery after interventions in these individuals. For deeper analysis of contributing elements, the cohort was split retrospectively and randomly into training (n=68, 70%) and validation (n=30, 30%) groups. Leveraging training set information, both univariate and multivariate logistic regressions enabled the formulation of a nomogram to forecast healing post-revascularization in Rutherford grade 5 ischemia. Assessment of the model's effectiveness involved ROC evaluations, calibration assessments, and decision curve analysis (DCA). Results: The results showed that the TyG index was statistically significant in Rutherford grade 5 patients (p=0.011). Univariate analysis indicated that the TyG index was an independent risk factor (OR: 3.96, 95% CI: 1.33-11.73, p=0.013), and it’s area under ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT ARTICLE IN PRESS ARTICLE IN PRESS 3 the ROC curve (AUC) for predicting delayed wound healing was 0.68, with a best cutoff value of 8.83, sensitivity of 67.1%, and specificity of 71.4%. In the training cohort, the TyG index, triglyceride (TG), and smoking status were identified as independent predictors of wound healing after endovascular treatment in Rutherford grade 5 patients (all p < 0.05). A nomogram was constructed using these three variables, demonstrating an AUC of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.71-0.95) in the training set and 0.68 (95% CI: 0.45-0.91) in the validation set, with good calibration observed in both cohorts. DCA indicated that this model could provide additional net clinical benefit in the low cost-effectiveness ratio threshold range. Conclusion: The TyG index may be an independent risk factor for delayed wound healing in Rutherford grade 5 patients following endovascular therapy. The nomogram model incorporating TyG index, TG levels, and smoking status demonstrates good predictive performance for wound healing after revascularization in these patients, and may positively impact early diagnosis/treatment, prevention of overtreatment, and precision medicine with optimized resource allocation.
